opus-5.5.text:
I think the number of players at the very top will keep shrinking. Training frontier models is getting more expensive, not less, in compute, data, and especially talent density, so maybe only a handful of companies globally can sustain it. That's true on both the open and closed sides.

But I don't think the open-versus-closed split will collapse into one camp. Open source has proven much more durable than many people expected two or three years ago. Open models now come close to the frontier, sometimes within months, and that changes the dynamics. For a company like ours, open-sourcing isn't charity. It's a way to build influence, attract developers, get feedback at a scale you can't get internally, and become part of the infrastructure that everyone else builds on.

So my guess is a small number of closed frontier labs, mostly in the US, pushing the absolute capability ceiling. Alongside them, a small number of very strong open-source players, many of them Chinese, setting the baseline for everyone else. Around those two groups there will be a very long tail of companies doing fine-tuning, agents, and applications, but not really competing at the base-model level.

The key question isn't how many players there are. It's whether you can keep up with the frontier. The gap can open or close quickly. When a new paradigm appears, like reasoning or agentic RL, it reshuffles things for a while. What matters is whether you can turn compute into intelligence efficiently and keep doing it. The teams that can do that will survive, whether they're open or closed. The ones that can't will gradually turn into application companies, and that's not necessarily a bad outcome.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts that only a handful of companies will sustain frontier training, with a small number of leading open and closed players and a long tail focused on applications.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two will coexist, but the numbers will look very different on each side.

On the closed-source side, the count will keep shrinking. Training a frontier model is now an enormous bet on compute, data, and talent, and each generation raises the bar again. Only a handful of players can keep up with that, maybe three to five in the US and a similar small number in China. Everyone else either falls a generation behind or decides it's no longer worth trying to compete at the very top. So globally I'd expect a single-digit number of companies that genuinely sit at the frontier.

Open source is more interesting. In the long run there probably won't be many organizations that can afford to train a top-tier open model from scratch either, because the cost structure is the same. But the ecosystem built on top of open models will be much wider: fine-tuning, distillation, vertical applications, agents. So you'll have a few base-model providers and then thousands of players downstream.

The gap between the two camps will keep oscillating. Open models will stay roughly one generation behind the best closed models, sometimes catching up, sometimes falling further behind depending on how fast the frontier moves. What matters for a company like ours is not open versus closed as an ideology, but whether you can stay at the frontier. If you're not pushing the boundary yourself, your choice between the two won't matter much.

r001.rationale: The response predicts fewer closed-source frontier providers and says only a few organizations will be able to train top-tier open models, indicating increasing concentration among model providers.

astra-6.text:
I think the number of companies training frontier models will probably shrink, whether they’re open-source or closed-source. The investment required—in compute, talent, and infrastructure—keeps increasing, so it’s difficult for a large number of players to stay at the frontier.

But if you look at the number of companies building on those models, I expect that to grow substantially. Open-source makes it possible for more teams to adapt models and build products without training everything from scratch.

So I’d distinguish between a relatively small number of foundational model providers and a much larger ecosystem of developers. I also don’t think open-source and closed-source will be two completely separate camps. A company can release some models openly while keeping others proprietary. Both approaches can coexist, and the balance will depend on model quality, cost, and how companies capture value.

r001.rationale: The response predicts fewer companies will train frontier models and describes foundational model providers as a relatively small group, citing rising investment requirements. This communicates increasing concentration among global AI providers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see some concentration at the frontier, because training the strongest models requires a lot of capital, compute, and research talent. There may be only a handful of organizations globally that can consistently push that frontier, whether they release their models openly or keep them closed.

But if we’re talking about the number of companies building on those models, that could grow substantially. Open-source models lower the barrier to entry, so more teams can adapt them to particular industries or user needs without training everything from scratch.

I also don’t think open and closed will be two fixed camps. A company might release some models openly and keep others proprietary. So my expectation is fewer players competing on foundational model capability, but a much broader ecosystem competing on products and applications.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that only a handful of organizations globally will consistently push the frontier, whether their models are open or closed, and summarizes this as fewer players competing on foundational model capability.
